Top Nav

The 40px corporate utility strip that sits above the product header: Iron Software lockup and company-level menu on the left, office address, Contact Us and the language picker on the right. Pair it above Product Menu for the full two-bar header.

2 variants40px stripFigma 507:5349

Default

Filled with --slate-800. The standard treatment on light pages.

Transparent

Figma’s “Without bg”. No fill, so the strip sits directly over a hero image or dark section. Check contrast against whatever sits behind it — the labels are white and get no scrim of their own.

Responsive

The navigation canvas in Figma is 1440 desktop only, so unlike Footer Bar there is no md or sm frame to match — what this component does as it narrows is an implementation decision, not a drawn one. It hides the address below 1100 and the menu below 720. Neither number is on the project’s breakpoint scale (--breakpoint-md 768, --breakpoint-lg 1024), which is worth knowing before anyone treats them as settled.
The preview is an <iframe> loading this same page at ?frame=, because an iframe is the only box on a page with a viewport of its own — the demo frames above are pinned to 1440 by .frame-scroll and will never show this. Nothing is duplicated to make it work.
1024px
Drag the handle across 1100 and 720 to watch each element go. The presets are deliberately not this component’s own thresholds, so the gap between the two is visible: at the --breakpoint-lg preset of 1024 the address is already gone, and at --breakpoint-md 768 the menu is still there with 48px to spare. The handle takes arrow keys (±16, or ±1 with Shift), which is the only reliable way to land on an exact threshold.

Code

// the full two-bar header
<TopNav items={[
  { label: 'Products', href: '/products' },
  { label: 'Enterprise' },
  { label: 'Solutions' },
  { label: 'Resources' },
  { label: 'About US' },
]} />
<ProductMenu product="pdf" productName="PDF" items={menu} />

// over a hero image
<TopNav variant="transparent" items={items} />

// region-neutral, single locale
<TopNav items={items} showAddress={false} showLanguage={false} />
<div class="tn tn--default">
  <nav class="tn-inner" aria-label="Corporate">
    <div class="tn-left">
      <a class="tn-brand" href="/">
        <svg class="tn-mark">…</svg>
        <span class="tn-brand-text"><b>IRON</b><span>SOFTWARE</span></span>
      </a>
      <ul class="tn-menu">
        <li><a class="tn-item">Products <svg class="tn-caret">…</svg></a></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="tn-right">
      <span class="tn-address"><svg class="tn-pin">…</svg>205 N. Michigan Ave. …</span>
      <a class="tn-item">Contact Us</a>
      <span class="tn-lang"><svg class="tn-globe">…</svg><a class="tn-item">EN</a></span>
    </div>
  </nav>
</div>

Guidelines

✓ Do
  • Keep this strip for company-level destinations — product navigation belongs in Product Menu below it.
  • Check contrast behind transparent; the labels are white with no scrim of their own.
  • Drop the address before the menu when space runs out — it is the longest and least navigational item.
✗ Don't
  • Don’t recolour the Iron Software mark to white — it is --color-neutral here by design, recessive next to the wordmark.
  • Don’t use this strip on its own as a page’s only navigation.
  • Don’t stack more corporate links in; five is what the design budgets for at 1440px.

Notes

Figma specifies 1440px desktop only. The narrow-viewport behaviour here — the address goes at 1100px, the corporate menu at 720px — is an implementation decision, not a handed-over design.

Figma sets gap: 0 between a label and its caret and lets the caret’s own 16×16 box provide the spacing. The caret SVG therefore uses an offset viewBox to centre its 6.2×3.8 triangle inside 16×16, rather than adding a wrapper element.
